classification.difficultyReason: Use the two equal-tangent pairs and point order to subtract direct tangent segments, then construct crossing tangents and adapt the argument to sums.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Each tangent, FR and GS, in the diagram is called a direct common tangent because the two circles lie on the same side of the tangent. Produce the two tangents to meet at M.

spec.description: Two separate circles on same side of each direct common tangent; F,R,M and G,S,M have correct order. No centres/radii added.
spec.answerVisibility: Original supplied givens and targets only; no derived numerical values or proof conclusions.

answer.worked: For the larger circle, MF and MG are tangents from the same external point M, so MF=MG. For the smaller circle, MR and MS are tangents from M, so MR=MS.

F,R,M are collinear in that order and G,S,M are collinear in that order. Hence
$$\begin{align*}FR&=MF-MR\\&=MG-MS\\&=GS.\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Draw a diagram showing indirect common tangents, and prove that they also have equal length. (Note: Indirect common tangents cross over, and intersect between the two circles.)

answer.short: The two indirect common tangent segments are equal: $FS=GR$.
answer.worked:
Let FS and GR be the indirect common tangents, intersecting at M between the circles. Tangents from M to the left circle give MF=MG; tangents from M to the right circle give MS=MR. Therefore
$$\begin{align*}FS&=FM+MS\\&=GM+MR\\&=GR.\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Indirect common tangents FS and GR cross between circles at M. Equal tangent pairs give FS=FM+MS and GR=GM+MR.
